items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "symbol".
items.answer: Something – an object, gesture, word or image – that stands for something else by convention, so that its meaning must be learned
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: something – an object, gesture, word or image – that stands for something else by convention, so that its meaning must be learned. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between culture as shared and culture as contested.
items.answer: Seeing culture as shared emphasises common values that hold a group together; seeing it as contested emphasises disagreement, power and change, as different members claim and redefine what "our culture" is.
items.markingKey: Seeing culture as shared emphasises common values that hold a group together; seeing it as contested emphasises disagreement, power and change, as different members claim and redefine what "our culture" is. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why culture is said to be symbolic.
items.answer: Humans relate to the world through shared, learned meanings: a gesture, colour or object (e.g. a wedding ring) has meaning only by convention, so understanding behaviour requires grasping the symbols involved.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Humans relate to the world through shared, learned meanings: a gesture, colour or object (e.g. a wedding ring) has meaning only by convention, so understanding behaviour requires grasping the symbols involved. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the text below.

Every December the elders of the Nakamura neighbourhood association repair the paper lanterns for the shrine festival. This year the young men who carry the portable shrine asked to add LED strips. Mr Kato, who has led the festival for thirty years, refused: "The flame must flicker. That is how the kami know we are here." His granddaughter, filming on her phone, rolled her eyes. "He says the same thing about the music, but he changed the route when the new road came." In the end, the LEDs were allowed on the trucks that follow the shrine, but not on the shrine itself.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a neighbourhood shrine festival in urban Japan.

Using the key concept of culture, explain how the text shows culture as contested rather than simply shared. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: Members of the same community disagree about what the tradition requires: an elder with authority defends a symbolic meaning (the flicker communicates with the kami), younger people propose change, and the granddaughter exposes that tradition has already been adapted. The compromise shows culture being negotiated through power (seniority) and change.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Members of the same community disagree about what the tradition requires: an elder with authority defends a symbolic meaning (the flicker communicates with the kami), younger people propose change, and the granddaughter exposes that tradition has already been adapted. The compromise shows culture being negotiated through power (seniority) and change. Markbands – 4: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 2–3: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: A student claims: "Culture is something people are born with because it is passed down through families." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Culture is learned through enculturation; families transmit it socially, not genetically, and people can acquire new cultures.
items.markingKey: Culture is learned through enculturation; families transmit it socially, not genetically, and people can acquire new cultures. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to one anthropological text you have studied, for example Wolf's Europe and the People Without History, explain the relevance of change to the learning, sharing and contesting of culture.
items.answer: He rejected the image of timeless "people without history", insisting that all societies have been transformed by connections with others.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: He rejected the image of timeless "people without history", insisting that all societies have been transformed by connections with others. Award up to [5]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Eric Wolf, Europe and the People Without History (1982), in a Marxist historical anthropology of global capitalism from 1400 to 1900); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to change. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

With reference to the text and to professional guidelines such as the AAA Principles of Professional Responsibility, discuss the ethical responsibilities of the anthropologist. Suggest how the anthropologist might respond to the dilemmas you identify.
items.answer: Filming and quoting identifiable people in a small neighbourhood association could create family or community conflict; consent from Mr Kato and the granddaughter, careful use of video and anonymisation of the neighbourhood are needed, as is sensitivity to sacred practices. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

With reference to culture, compare and contrast the text with one ethnography you have studied. You might choose Mead's Coming of Age in Samoa. Make sure you contextualise the ethnography: author, people, place and time.
items.answer: Text: Members of the same community disagree about what the tradition requires: an elder with authority defends a symbolic meaning (the flicker communicates with the kami), younger people propose change, and the granddaughter exposes that tradition has already been adapted. The compromise shows culture being negotiated through power (seniority) and change. Ethnography – Margaret Mead, Coming of Age in Samoa (1928), among adolescent girls on Ta'ū in the Manu'a Islands of American Samoa (fieldwork 1925–1926): Mead argued that adolescence in Samoa was relatively free of the stress seen in the United States, supporting Boas's view that culture rather than biology shapes development; Derek Freeman's 1983 critique disputed her findings. Comparison: similarities and differences in how culture is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Explain why many anthropologists now describe culture as contested rather than simply shared.
items.answer: Within any group people differ by gender, age, class and power, and they argue over values and practices; treating culture as uniformly shared hides these differences and often privileges the views of dominant members.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Within any group people differ by gender, age, class and power, and they argue over values and practices; treating culture as uniformly shared hides these differences and often privileges the views of dominant members. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between Tylor's definition of culture and Geertz's definition of culture.
items.answer: Tylor treated culture as a complex whole of acquired capabilities, arranged on an evolutionary scale; Geertz treated culture as public webs of meaning to be interpreted through thick description, with no evolutionary ranking.
items.markingKey: Tylor treated culture as a complex whole of acquired capabilities, arranged on an evolutionary scale; Geertz treated culture as public webs of meaning to be interpreted through thick description, with no evolutionary ranking. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Mead's Coming of Age in Samoa and Freeman's critique shows debates about culture versus biology.
items.answer: Mead (1928) portrayed Samoan adolescence as relatively untroubled; Derek Freeman (1983) argued she had been misled and ignored violence and strict sexual norms. The controversy shows how claims about culture can be contested and how the ethnographer's theory and informants shape what is found.
items.markingKey: Context (Mead (1928) portrayed Samoan adolescence as relatively untroubled; Derek Freeman (1983) argued she had been misled and ignored violence and strict sexual norms.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the controversy shows how claims about culture can be contested and how the ethnographer's theory and informants shape what is found. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to debates about culture versus biology.

items.stem: Define the term "identity".
items.answer: The sense of who a person or group is, constructed through self-identification and recognition (or ascription) by others
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the sense of who a person or group is, constructed through self-identification and recognition (or ascription) by others. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an achieved identity and an ascribed identity.
items.answer: An ascribed identity is assigned by birth or by others (e.g. caste, nationality at birth); an achieved identity is gained through actions or choices (e.g. becoming a doctor, converting religion), though the line between them is often blurred.
items.markingKey: An ascribed identity is assigned by birth or by others (e.g. caste, nationality at birth); an achieved identity is gained through actions or choices (e.g. becoming a doctor, converting religion), though the line between them is often blurred. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why belonging always involves exclusion.
items.answer: Defining who belongs to a group, nation or place requires boundaries that mark others as outsiders, as Barth showed for ethnic groups and as citizenship rules show for nations.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Defining who belongs to a group, nation or place requires boundaries that mark others as outsiders, as Barth showed for ethnic groups and as citizenship rules show for nations. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to Serena Nanda, Neither Man nor Woman: The Hijras of India (1990), explain how the key concept of identity helps us to understand the formation of identities based on ethnicity, gender, class and nation.
items.answer: Hijras are culturally recognised as neither man nor woman, a third gender with a ritual role linked to devotion to the goddess Bahuchara Mata.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Hijras are culturally recognised as neither man nor woman, a third gender with a ritual role linked to devotion to the goddess Bahuchara Mata. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Serena Nanda, Neither Man nor Woman: The Hijras of India (1990), among hijra communities in India); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to identity. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Using Bourgois's study of crack dealers in East Harlem as an example, explain intersections of class, ethnicity and gender in identity.
items.answer: Young Puerto Rican men refused humiliating office jobs and sought respect through street culture. Their identity as respected men was shaped by class marginality, ethnic discrimination and masculine ideals, showing identities intersect.
items.markingKey: Context (Young Puerto Rican men refused humiliating office jobs and sought respect through street culture.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: their identity as respected men was shaped by class marginality, ethnic discrimination and masculine ideals, showing identities intersect. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to intersections of class, ethnicity and gender in identity.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Identity is chosen by individuals rather than imposed by society."
items.answer: Identity is negotiated: individuals choose within limits set by classification, power and recognition by others.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: people perform and switch identities situationally (Malkki's town refugees); online and urban life offer new identity options. Arguments against: ascribed categories such as caste, race and citizenship are imposed by states and others; symbolic violence makes imposed identities feel natural (Holmes); structural constraints shape what is possible (Bourgois). Supported judgement: Identity is negotiated: individuals choose within limits set by classification, power and recognition by others.

items.stem: Fredrik Barth's Ethnic Groups and Boundaries (1969) argued that ethnic groups are defined mainly by:
options: the cultural traits shared inside each group
the social boundaries maintained between groups
items.answer: the social boundaries maintained between groups
items.markingKey: D. Barth shifted attention from "cultural stuff" to boundary maintenance.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

At the football academy, the coach divides the boys into "locals" and "internationals" for the Saturday match. Tomasz, born in the city to Polish parents, plays for the internationals. "At home I am Polish, at school I am British, here I am international," he shrugs. The local boys tease the internationals by imitating accents, but when the academy plays a team from the next town, everyone sings the same chant. After the match, the parents stand in separate groups by the car park: Polish, Somali, and "the English ones", as Tomasz's mother calls them.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a youth football academy in an English city.

Identify and describe how Tomasz describes his identity. Refer closely to the text. You do not need to refer to any other ethnography in this answer.
items.answer: He says he is Polish at home, British at school and "international" at the academy; he was born in the city to Polish parents; he is placed by the coach in the internationals group; he shrugs, suggesting identities are routine and situational.
items.markingKey: He says he is Polish at home, British at school and "international" at the academy; he was born in the city to Polish parents; he is placed by the coach in the internationals group; he shrugs, suggesting identities are routine and situational. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: "Ethnic identity is mainly a product of boundaries rather than of shared culture." Discuss with reference to at least one ethnography you have studied.
items.answer: Boundaries are central, but shared memories and state classification also shape ethnicity.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Barth's argument that boundaries persist despite cultural change; ethnic markers are selected and changed strategically; shared language, history and practices give ethnicity emotional force; states and censuses also create ethnic categories from above. Suitable ethnographies include Barth's Ethnic Groups and Boundaries, Abu-Lughod's Veiled Sentiments, Bourgois's In Search of Respect. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Boundaries are central, but shared memories and state classification also shape ethnicity. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The expected behaviour attached to a social status"?
items.answer: role
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of role.

items.stem: Briefly explain why exchange creates social relations.
items.answer: Gifts create obligations to receive and repay (Mauss); the return keeps a relationship alive, as with kula partners, so exchange is a way of making and maintaining ties, not only transferring goods.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Gifts create obligations to receive and repay (Mauss); the return keeps a relationship alive, as with kula partners, so exchange is a way of making and maintaining ties, not only transferring goods. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "In kin-based societies people have no individual choice because their roles are fixed." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Even where kinship organises roles, people negotiate, manipulate and contest them – for example by choosing which kin to rely on or which obligations to honour.
items.markingKey: Even where kinship organises roles, people negotiate, manipulate and contest them – for example by choosing which kin to rely on or which obligations to honour. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the kula ring described by Malinowski, explain how it illustrates exchange as the basis of social relations.
items.answer: Trobriand men maintained lifelong exchange partners on other islands through which shell valuables circulated in opposite directions. The gifts create durable obligations and alliances between islands, showing exchange producing social structure.
items.markingKey: Context (Trobriand men maintained lifelong exchange partners on other islands through which shell valuables circulated in opposite directions.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the gifts create durable obligations and alliances between islands, showing exchange producing social structure. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to exchange as the basis of social relations.

items.stem: Identify one way in which power matters in Bourdieu's Outline of a Theory of Practice (based on fieldwork among the Kabyle of Algeria (1950s–1960s)) and explain its significance.
items.answer: Bourdieu showed how domination is reproduced through habitus – embodied dispositions that make inequality feel natural (doxa) – and through symbolic capital such as honour.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Bourdieu showed how domination is reproduced through habitus – embodied dispositions that make inequality feel natural (doxa) – and through symbolic capital such as honour. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Pierre Bourdieu, Outline of a Theory of Practice (1972; English 1977), based on fieldwork among the Kabyle of Algeria (1950s–1960s)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to power. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Social structure determines individual behaviour."
items.answer: Structure strongly constrains behaviour but is itself reproduced and modified through people's practices.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: institutions and roles shape expectations from birth; structural-functionalists such as Radcliffe-Brown emphasised stability. Arguments against: people negotiate and change roles (Abu-Lughod's poets, Scott's resisting peasants); Bourdieu's practice theory shows structure reproduced through agents' practices, which can change it. Supported judgement: Structure strongly constrains behaviour but is itself reproduced and modified through people's practices.

items.stem: Explain why anthropologists distinguish between status and role.
items.answer: Status is the position a person occupies, while role is the behaviour expected of it; the distinction lets anthropologists analyse how people perform, stretch or fail to meet expectations of a position.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Status is the position a person occupies, while role is the behaviour expected of it; the distinction lets anthropologists analyse how people perform, stretch or fail to meet expectations of a position. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the tower block, the WhatsApp group "Floor 9 Aunties" has forty-two members. Mrs Okafor, who has lived there longest, posts each morning: who needs a lift to the clinic, whose son has a job interview. When the lift broke for a week, members took turns carrying shopping for Mr Lindqvist, the retired sailor on the top floor. "We don't keep accounts," says Mrs Okafor, "but everyone knows who helps." New tenants are added only after someone has "met them properly". Last year a young man was removed from the group after he refused to lend his ladder.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a council housing block in a European city.

Using the key concept of social relations, explain how the WhatsApp group creates and regulates social relations. Use appropriate anthropological terminology throughout your answer.
items.answer: The group is a network that redistributes help through generalised reciprocity ("we don't keep accounts") yet reputation tracks who helps; Mrs Okafor's long residence gives her status and a coordinating role; admission and removal (the ladder) show boundaries and sanctions that enforce obligations.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The group is a network that redistributes help through generalised reciprocity ("we don't keep accounts") yet reputation tracks who helps; Mrs Okafor's long residence gives her status and a coordinating role; admission and removal (the ladder) show boundaries and sanctions that enforce obligations. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Who edited The Social Life of Things (1986), arguing that objects have biographies?
items.answer: Arjun Appadurai
items.markingKey: C. Appadurai's introduction argues that things move in and out of the commodity state.

items.stem: Explain why a gift is not the same as a commodity.
items.answer: A commodity transfer ends the relationship once paid for, whereas a gift creates an obligation to reciprocate and so maintains a relationship and carries the identity of the giver.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A commodity transfer ends the relationship once paid for, whereas a gift creates an obligation to reciprocate and so maintains a relationship and carries the identity of the giver. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to Weiner's study of Trobriand women's wealth, explain how it illustrates materiality and gendered power.
items.answer: At mortuary ceremonies women distributed thousands of banana-leaf bundles and fibre skirts to repay those who had cared for the dead. Objects with little use value became the means through which women displayed status and regenerated matrilineal identity.
items.markingKey: Context (At mortuary ceremonies women distributed thousands of banana-leaf bundles and fibre skirts to repay those who had cared for the dead.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: objects with little use value became the means through which women displayed status and regenerated matrilineal identity. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to materiality and gendered power.

items.stem: "Material culture only tells us about technology, not about meaning." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Objects encode meanings, relationships and power: Weiner's banana-leaf bundles express matrilineal identity and women's power.
items.markingKey: Objects encode meanings, relationships and power: Weiner's banana-leaf bundles express matrilineal identity and women's power. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In Hanh's family altar room in Ho Chi Minh City, a plastic Rolex sits beside her grandfather's photograph. Every year on the anniversary of his death, the family burn paper replicas – a motorbike, a smartphone, US dollars – so he can use them "on the other side". Hanh buys them from a shop on Hàng Mã street that also sells paper iPads. Her brother, who works in Singapore, sends money for the best models. "My grandfather never had a watch when he was alive," Hanh says. "Now he is a rich man."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a household in Vietnam.

Compare the significance of materiality in the text with its significance in De León's The Land of Open Graves. Refer explicitly to the ethnographic context of both. Make sure you contextualise the ethnography: author, people, place and time.
items.answer: Text: Burning paper goods transfers them to the ancestor, so objects maintain an ongoing exchange relationship across death; choosing luxury items expresses care and raises the grandfather's (and family's) status; migrant remittances finance the ritual, linking transnational family ties to ancestor care; consumer modernity is absorbed into ritual. Ethnography – Jason De León, The Land of Open Graves: Living and Dying on the Migrant Trail (2015), on the US–Mexico border in the Sonoran Desert, Arizona, through the Undocumented Migration Project: De León combines archaeology, forensic science and ethnography, analysing discarded water bottles, backpacks and clothing as traces of migrants' experience. Comparison: similarities and differences in how materiality is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Text: Burning paper goods transfers them to the ancestor, so objects maintain an ongoing exchange relationship across death; choosing luxury items expresses care and raises the grandfather's (and family's) status; migrant remittances finance the ritual, linking transnational family ties to ancestor care; consumer modernity is absorbed into ritual. Ethnography – Jason De León, The Land of Open Graves: Living and Dying on the Migrant Trail (2015), on the US–Mexico border in the Sonoran Desert, Arizona, through the Undocumented Migration Project: De León combines archaeology, forensic science and ethnography, analysing discarded water bottles, backpacks and clothing as traces of migrants' experience. Comparison: similarities and differences in how materiality is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them. Any well-contextualised ethnography is acceptable. items.stem: Explain why objects can change meaning as they move.
items.answer: Value depends on context: a mass-produced item becomes a gift, an heirloom or a museum piece, gaining new meanings through the relationships and histories attached to it (Appadurai).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Value depends on context: a mass-produced item becomes a gift, an heirloom or a museum piece, gaining new meanings through the relationships and histories attached to it (Appadurai). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that global consumer goods are making cultures more alike? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: Global goods spread, but local appropriation means they often increase diversity of meaning rather than homogenise.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: the same brands and phones are found worldwide; consumption of global goods can displace local crafts; people localise goods, giving them new meanings (Why We Post); second-hand clothing and phones are used in culturally specific ways. Suitable ethnographies include Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific, Weiner's Women of Value, Men of Renown, Miller's studies of shopping and household objects. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Global goods spread, but local appropriation means they often increase diversity of meaning rather than homogenise. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The process by which a person learns the norms, values and practices of their culture, mainly in childhood"?
items.answer: enculturation
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of enculturation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The sense of who a person or group is, constructed through self-identification and recognition (or ascription) by others"?
items.answer: identity
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of identity.

items.stem: Which anthropologist is associated with the structural-functionalist view of society as a system of social relations?
items.answer: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown
items.markingKey: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown. Radcliffe-Brown analysed social structure as a network of relations maintaining society.

items.stem: Distinguish between a commodity and a gift.
items.answer: A gift is embedded in relationships and creates obligation and identity links between giver and receiver; a commodity is exchanged impersonally for a price, ending the relationship once the transaction is complete.
items.markingKey: A gift is embedded in relationships and creates obligation and identity links between giver and receiver; a commodity is exchanged impersonally for a price, ending the relationship once the transaction is complete. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "All members of a culture share exactly the same beliefs." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Culture is shared in part but also contested: Abu-Lughod showed Awlad 'Ali Bedouin voicing sentiments in poetry that contradicted the public honour code.

items.stem: Maya writes: "Gender is simply determined by biological sex in all societies." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Gender is culturally constructed: societies recognise different gender categories and roles, such as hijras in India.

items.stem: Explain the difference between generalised reciprocity and balanced reciprocity.
items.answer: Generalised reciprocity is giving without expecting a specific or immediate return, usual among close kin; balanced reciprocity expects an equivalent return within a set time, usual between more distant equals.

items.stem: A student claims: "Consumption is a purely individual and selfish activity." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Miller showed shopping as care for others, and consumption often expresses and builds social relationships and group identities.

At the football academy, the coach divides the boys into "locals" and "internationals" for the Saturday match. Tomasz, born in the city to Polish parents, plays for the internationals. "At home I am Polish, at school I am British, here I am international," he shrugs. The local boys tease the internationals by imitating accents, but when the academy plays a team from the next town, everyone sings the same chant. After the match, the parents stand in separate groups by the car park: Polish, Somali, and "the English ones", as Tomasz's mother calls them.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a youth football academy in an English city.

items.answer: The coach's classification (locals/internationals) creates groups; teasing about accents marks boundaries (Barth); a shared chant against another town shows a wider "us" that includes everyone (situational belonging); parents' separation by nationality shows boundaries persisting in adult social relations.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the tower block, the WhatsApp group "Floor 9 Aunties" has forty-two members. Mrs Okafor, who has lived there longest, posts each morning: who needs a lift to the clinic, whose son has a job interview. When the lift broke for a week, members took turns carrying shopping for Mr Lindqvist, the retired sailor on the top floor. "We don't keep accounts," says Mrs Okafor, "but everyone knows who helps." New tenants are added only after someone has "met them properly". Last year a young man was removed from the group after he refused to lend his ladder.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a council housing block in a European city.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In Hanh's family altar room in Ho Chi Minh City, a plastic Rolex sits beside her grandfather's photograph. Every year on the anniversary of his death, the family burn paper replicas – a motorbike, a smartphone, US dollars – so he can use them "on the other side". Hanh buys them from a shop on Hàng Mã street that also sells paper iPads. Her brother, who works in Singapore, sends money for the best models. "My grandfather never had a watch when he was alive," Hanh says. "Now he is a rich man."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a household in Vietnam.

With reference to the concept of materiality, analyse how material objects sustain relationships between the living and the dead in the text. You may consider more than one possible interpretation of the evidence.
items.answer: Burning paper goods transfers them to the ancestor, so objects maintain an ongoing exchange relationship across death; choosing luxury items expresses care and raises the grandfather's (and family's) status; migrant remittances finance the ritual, linking transnational family ties to ancestor care; consumer modernity is absorbed into ritual.

Every December the elders of the Nakamura neighbourhood association repair the paper lanterns for the shrine festival. This year the young men who carry the portable shrine asked to add LED strips. Mr Kato, who has led the festival for thirty years, refused: "The flame must flicker. That is how the kami know we are here." His granddaughter, filming on her phone, rolled her eyes. "He says the same thing about the music, but he changed the route when the new road came." In the end, the LEDs were allowed on the trucks that follow the shrine, but not on the shrine itself.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a neighbourhood shrine festival in urban Japan.

items.stem: With reference to Stack's study of "The Flats", explain how it illustrates networks as social structure.
items.answer: Women swapped food, money and childcare across households, and welfare rules discouraged marriage and saving. Domestic life was organised through networks rather than nuclear households, and state rules shaped these relations.

items.stem: Outline how materiality shapes the use and exchange of objects, using evidence from Miller's studies of shopping and household objects.
items.answer: Miller argued that everyday shopping is largely an act of love and sacrifice for family members, and that the objects people keep at home express and sustain their relationships.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Geertz's interpretive approach is the most useful way to understand culture."
items.answer: Interpretation is essential, but it is most useful when combined with attention to power, history and internal disagreement.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: thick description captures meanings from the actors' point of view; it treats culture as public and observable rather than hidden in minds. Arguments against: it can neglect power and inequality (critiqued by Asad and Roseberry); the ethnographer's interpretation may be privileged over participants' own; it can present a culture as more coherent than it is. Supported judgement: Interpretation is essential, but it is most useful when combined with attention to power, history and internal disagreement.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "symbol"?
options: Annette Weiner's term for objects that cannot be given away permanently because they embody a group's identity, such as heirlooms or sacred objects
The idea, developed by Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989), that identities such as gender, race and class interact to produce particular experiences of privilege or disadvantage
Something – an object, gesture, word or image – that stands for something else by convention, so that its meaning must be learned
The expected behaviour attached to a social status

options: Geertz's term for ethnographic writing that interprets the layered meanings of an action for those involved, rather than just recording behaviour
A form of identity based on a claimed shared origin, history or culture, which is maintained through boundaries between "us" and "them"
Thorstein Veblen's term (1899) for spending on visible goods to display wealth and status
A thing produced or acquired for exchange, usually through the market, whose value is expressed in price

items.answer: Culture is learned through enculturation; families transmit it socially, not genetically, and people can acquire new cultures.

items.stem: Briefly describe Malkki's research with Hutu refugees in Tanzania (1985–1986) and explain what it reveals about identity as situational and shaped by place.
items.answer: Refugees in Mishamo camp narrated a "mythico-history" of themselves as the true Hutu nation in exile, while refugees in Kigoma town blended in and avoided the refugee label. items.stem: With reference to two anthropological studies, such as Boas's historical particularism and Geertz's "Deep Play", compare and contrast the role of culture in the learning, sharing and contesting of culture.
items.answer: Boas's historical particularism (in his work on the Kwakwaka'wakw of British Columbia and on immigrants in New York): Boas argued that each culture is the product of its own history and must be understood in its own terms (historical particularism), rejecting rankings of cultures as "savage" or "civilised". Geertz's "Deep Play" (in a Balinese village (fieldwork with Hildred Geertz, 1958)): Geertz read the cockfight as a text – "a story they tell themselves about themselves" – to be interpreted through thick description of its layered meanings. items.stem: Big question: "Can an anthropologist ever fully understand another way of life?" Discuss with reference to the key concept of identity and at least one ethnography you have studied, such as Nanda's Neither Man nor Woman.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies identity explicitly and uses ethnography: Hijras are culturally recognised as neither man nor woman, a third gender with a ritual role linked to devotion to the goddess Bahuchara Mata. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.

items.stem: With reference to two anthropological studies, such as Bourdieu's Outline of a Theory of Practice and Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific, compare and contrast the role of social relations in the organisation of roles, status and networks.
items.answer: Bourdieu's Outline of a Theory of Practice (based on fieldwork among the Kabyle of Algeria (1950s–1960s)): Gift exchange depends on a time interval between gift and counter-gift, which disguises self-interest and turns exchange into honour and obligation. Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific (among the Trobriand Islanders of Papua New Guinea (fieldwork 1915–1918)): In the kula ring, men on different islands keep lifelong partnerships through the ceremonial exchange of shell valuables: soulava necklaces travel clockwise and mwali armshells anticlockwise, creating alliances between communities rather than profit. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far social relations is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: Using Weiner's Women of Value, Men of Renown and Miller's studies of shopping and household objects, compare the ways in which materiality is experienced and contested by the people studied.
items.answer: Weiner's Women of Value, Men of Renown (in Kiriwina, Trobriand Islands, revisiting Malinowski's field site in the 1970s): Banana-leaf bundles have little use value but are essential in mortuary exchanges that restore the dead person's matrilineal (dala) identity, so humble objects carry cosmological value. Miller's studies of shopping and household objects (among households on streets in North London): Miller argued that everyday shopping is largely an act of love and sacrifice for family members, and that the objects people keep at home express and sustain their relationships. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far materiality is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.
